meta.title: Thomas Herbert Kokholm
meta.description: Engineer and technology executive working on VR- and AI-based training platforms for healthcare and welfare education. Business & Innovation Director at CoFlow Visuals, Horsens, Denmark.

identity.name: Thomas Herbert Kokholm
identity.headline: Director, Business & Innovation at CoFlow Visuals ApS
identity.tagline: Electrical engineer by training, executive by career, now building VR- and AI-based training platforms for healthcare and welfare education, and researching how simulation-based training can demonstrably build clinical competence.

paragraphs: I am an electrical engineer who spent twentyfive years leading technical organisations, and who came back to building. Along the way I have run units of up to ninety people, held executive roles across software, industrial technology and recruitment, and driven change programmes in both private companies and public institutions.

Today I lead product strategy, research collaboration and educational development at CoFlow Visuals, where we build VR- and AI-based training platforms for healthcare and welfare education. The work is done together with university colleges, university hospitals and research institutions, and I am responsible for the full technical architecture as well as the commercial side.

The thread through all of it is the same question: what does it take for a simulated encounter to produce real clinical competence, and how would you know? That is where the engineering, the pedagogy and the measurement have to meet.

A first empirical answer came from a completed VR pilot study with Aalborg University and UCN, funded by Erhvervsfyrtårn Life Science and co-financed by the European Union, with a paper in preparation. Building on that work, an industrial PhD is in preparation.

research.intro: Applied research carried out from industry, in collaboration with university colleges, university hospitals and universities. An industrial PhD is in preparation.

lines.title: Real-time conversational agents as simulated patients
lines.body: Speech-driven agents only work as training partners if the turn-taking feels like a conversation. That makes the unglamorous parts decisive: voice activity detection, endpointing, latency budgets. My current empirical work optimises these parameters specifically for clinical history-taking, where pauses carry meaning and cutting a student off changes what is being taught.

lines.title: Simulation architecture for clinical education
lines.body: How a simulation platform is built determines what it can teach and what it can measure. I work on the architecture that connects scenario design, learner interaction and evaluation, so that a training system produces usable evidence rather than only an experience.

lines.title: VR-based training in healthcare and welfare
lines.body: Immersive training is expensive to produce and easy to justify badly. The work here concerns where virtual reality earns its cost against simpler formats, and how to design for transfer rather than novelty. Includes a study protocol for VR-based dementia care training.

lines.title: Assessment and validation of AI-driven training
lines.body: If an AI system judges a learner's performance, the judgement itself needs validating. I work on construct validity and evaluation design for AI-assisted assessment, and on the question of what counts as adequate evidence before such a system is put in front of students.

lines.title: Security and data protection in educational health platforms
lines.body: Security has run through my whole career, from co-authoring the national IT security guidance for Danish hospitals and sitting on the DS 484 standards committee, to being responsible for the handling of health data in CoFlow's platforms today. My position is that security is a foundational discipline in software education, not a supplementary module.
